utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So thank you, Madam Usher. Good morning to you, Madam Registrar. If you would kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All the accused are here. From amongst the Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Haynes, Mr. Meek, Ms. Condon. I think that's about it. The Prosecution, it's Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Thayer. I understand there are some preliminaries you wish to raise, both the Prosecution and, I think, one Defence team. Yes. Good morning to you, Mr. Thayer. If you would kindly proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone. Mr. President, I wanted briefly to bring to the attention of the Trial Chamber a pattern that on this side we see emerging that we find a little troubling with respect to the list of exhibits to be used on cross-examination. This is something that at this point we believe merits bringing to the Court's attention on the record. Yesterday, during the cross-examination, I think, as we could all see, my friend used several what were obvious witness statements that had been furnished to him among a volume of other documents at the Defence's request and in the course of our Rule 68 review process. It was clear that my friend had intended to use those documents, knew exactly what sections he wanted to use. They are all ERN'd. None of them was on the list of exhibits to be used on cross-examination. I did not make an issue of it at the time for two reasons: One, I know my friend was eager to move and move along. I did not want to interrupt it with an argument of this kind at that time. Moreover, given that it was anonymous field recordings of people, some of whom's name I don't know and I still don't know, I thought that it was less of a substantive issue to address at that time. However, we have seen, in the recent past, other examples of teams simply not furnishing us a list of documents to be used on cross-examination; and, in this case, I just find it inexplicable, particularly from a team that such a formalistic approach to following the Rules, that that wasn't done in this case. We were sure that we would get a list of the documents after court. We were sent a copy of our entire disclosure log and a copy of a disclosure letter with no further indication, and it was only after that that we were furnished with a list of the documents which had clearly existed before. Another part of the troubling pattern is an e-mail we received from another team, which shall remain nameless, disclosing its list of exhibits with the following language: "Please be advised that this team may use, during its cross-examination of Witness PW-108, any document uploaded by the Prosecution or any of the Defence teams, as well as any other document that may prove to become relevant in the course of the witness's testimony, including the following," and there is one document listed. I think we all know that on this side we are not absolutists when it comes to the formalisms. We do our best, but we recognise that we have to be flexible. But I think we've reached a point where we really need compliance with both the letter and the spirit of the Court's very explicit order in this case, and this is not a mystery to anybody. This has been an issue in the past, and I just want to bring it to the Court's attention at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer. Mr. Bourgon. And after Mr. Bourgon, any other Defence team that may wish to intervene. Yes, Mr. Bourgon. Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. My response will be very short. One, I would have liked my colleague to tell me that he would address the Court this morning as a preliminary matter, which we were not informed of. Secondly, any documents that we used yesterday were documents obtained specifically for this witness, in close coordination with the Prosecution, documents that we had been looking for, that we requested to get, that we gave a list. Unfortunately, my colleague does not have the knowledge of the colleague that we had been dealing with all along, who is not in the courtroom today, and he would know that these documents, there are absolutely no surprise. And what is also very important is that on no less than three specific occasions, I told my colleague, "I will use at length the material you have provided us about 1992." And I told my colleague on at least three occasions, possibly more. Whether he believed me or he put any seriousness to what I informed him of, there has been absolutely -- nobody has been taken by surprise here. We've been working for months on this witness, and the Prosecution knows what we were looking at and what they gave us. And we gave them a list of all the documents that we were about to use, but we did not list those witness statements, but we told them that we would use the material they had provided us with in 1992. When it's a witness statement and when it is information, there is absolutely no obligation, we believe, for us to say we're going to use this paragraph of this witness statement because it is going to contradict the witness on a specific issue. These are matters for cross-examination, and I really fail to understand what my colleague is -- what his problems are this morning. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let me make myself clear, Mr. President. We were given --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As I understood you - one moment - because what Mr. Bourgon said intrinsically does minimise, actually, the gravity of this particular instance, but it still does not provide an answer to the general complaint that you raised; mainly, that this is not the only case where this has happened, but we have experienced over the past weeks, in particular, almost a constant practice of not providing you with documents that the Defence intended to use. But I think this is what we need to address most.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It minimises nothing. We disclosed volumes of material, much of it at the Defences' request. We disclosed the initial batch of what we considered possible Rule 68 material. That was followed up by numerous requests from the Defence, in which they asked for other statements, other material, other tape-recordings, volumes of material. To tell us that we may use any of that material, without specifying even the name of somebody, even the document or the interview, is in clear violation of the letter and the spirit of the Court's order. That would be like us saying, "Well, here's our 65 ter list. Go for it." That is not what we have been doing in this case. That is not the order that this Court has imposed on all parties, and that is exactly what happened here. And that is only underscored by my friend sending us our entire disclosure log, as well as a disclosure cover letter, saying, "Here's a CD with all the stuff you requested." If a document or a recording is going to be used, we are supposed to get a list of the documents or the items that our friends intend to use during the course of their cross-examination. We're not asking for line or page cites, but we're asking to be notified what the document is. That was not done, that was not done deliberately in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will not get into a debate with my friend this morning. I have more important matters to deal with. However, I will provide the Court with what we sent to my friend yesterday, and we sent him a list of material that had been provided to us by the Prosecution, and it was followed by an e-mail saying, "You're not specific enough," and then we sent them the names of the witnesses and the exact statements that we were referring to. However, Mr. President, it is very important to note that there is a significant difference, in our view, between a document we are going to use and information we are going to use to contradict a witness. Information that comes from statements or from material provided by the Prosecution is not the same as a document that we are going to use. And in this case, those witnesses that are there, my friend's colleague will be able to say, when he returns from his trip, that the sources that we have been using are the ones that have been disclosed to us by the Prosecution; and specifically the rest that we were looking for, we found very little in. What we were looking into is mostly the exact witnesses from the other cases that my friend's colleague provided to us, and I don't think there is no violation here, and even though my colleague might say we take a very legalistic approach, that is true. But unlike the Prosecution, which tells us it's on the EDS, millions and millions and millions of pages, and, "You've been disclosed and you've been on notice, and that's good enough for you," we received specific material at our request for a specific witness, and we informed our colleagues that we would be using this material from 1992 for a specific witness. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Our position is, first of all, we are sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis today because Judge Stole is not available. The other thing is we have come to the conclusion to close the discussion on this here at this point and exhort you and invite you to have a meeting amongst yourselves in the same spirit of cooperation that has been shown in the past, and try to iron out any differences that may exist amongst you on this matter, such as the point raised by Mr. Bourgon; for example, can information derived from a source which may be a document be distinguished and separated from the document itself? I think you need to sit down and talk on this, rather than involve us directly at this stage, knowing that you can reach an agreement. Secondly, the other approach that Mr. Thayer objected to, namely, the other e-mail from an unnamed Defence team, whether that should be an acceptable practice or not, I am sure that if you sit down and discuss amongst yourselves, you can come back to us with an acceptable agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, of course, the rule or the guideline that we indicated at the beginning of this trial remains valid, and the principle that derives from it is that not only should there be disclosure, which is based on reciprocity, but the disclosure ought to be as specific as possible. This is something that you need to observe, and it is in this spirit that any further disclosure ought to be. I understand, also, that one of the Defence teams, I don't know exactly which -- yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I'd like again to correct the same error in the transcripts from the September the 3rd. I tried to do that on September the 4th, but it was not done. This is page 668, line 6 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you mentioned this already.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's still not corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But it was not corrected on September the 4th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but sometimes it takes some time before we receive notice of the corrected official transcript, if you could call it that. I don't know, but I think the point was taken when you raised it last Monday or Tuesday, I don't know when it was, and I expect the relative correction to be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But please draw our attention if it's not made, say, by mid next week. But usually it takes some days before they come back to us with the necessary document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'll wait until the end of next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, Madam Registrar will pursue it according to what we have said, and thank you for pointing it out to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Going back to the previous issue, we told you that the essence of the guideline that we had established in the beginning ought to be followed in any case, and that there should be a specific disclosure of material to be used by the Defence, as specific as possible. We also invited you to meet and iron out any difference or differences in the interpretation of that guideline that may linger even now, more than a year after the beginning of this trial. If you do not come to an agreement, then the understanding is, of course, that we haven't buried it; then you come back to us, explain to us where the disagreement or disagreements lay, and we will then, if necessary, provide you with further guidelines. All right. Now, having said that, is there anything else? Nothing. Madam Usher, if you could kindly bring the witness in. Incidentally, we had promised to come back to you on your requests, joint requests, for some time in October to enable you to regroup and also reorganise your work because of the special difficulties that this case presents. You had asked for the entire week of the 1st to the 5th and the following Monday. We have given that a lot of consideration. We do appreciate that you are doing your best to proceed with the utmost celerity and that, indeed, this case presents difficulties, and we have come to the conclusion to grant you the break that you requested, with the understanding that it will be utilised as indicated by Mr. McCloskey in one of the sittings when this was discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome back. Mr. Bourgon will --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon will proceed with his cross-examination. He will then be followed by others. Mr. Bourgon, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: To begin this morning, I would like to address a few of the things you mentioned yesterday, which I believe require some clarification. I'll begin with you mentioned at page 913, lines 5 to 9. The reference, of course, is for my colleagues so they can follow. Answering a request related to your first alleged visit to Zvornik Brigade Command with your friend, you stated, and I quote: "That was the first time I went to the Command with that friend." My question is the following: Before this alleged visit with your friend, I suggest to you that you did have to go -- or you did have the opportunity to go to the Command alone or with other persons before that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had an opportunity, but I didn't go.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So it is your testimony then, sir, that you never went physically to the Zvornik Brigade Command before that first alleged visit with your friend; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there when this was still a shoe factory, and maybe informally when the barracks was being opened, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. The next thing I'd like to clarify is on page 915, lines 21 to 23, and that was in relation to questions I put to you concerning Commander Pandurevic. I would just like you to confirm that Commander Pandurevic was not present in the area of Zvornik when the war started; that is, let's say, from April, May and June of 1992. Are you able to confirm this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm this because I am not aware of any such detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will then say: Did you, by any chance, encounter Commander Pandurevic during those months? And I will be specific in terms of April, May and June of 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you -- again, with respect to Commander Pandurevic, I suggest to you that when he did arrive in the Zvornik area, that was to be in command of a regular unit, and that was, namely, the Zvornik Brigade of the VRS. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to see Commander Pandurevic with my friend. That was our intention, but we didn't find him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Maybe, sir, my question was not clear. I am talking now in 1992, and those are the months of April, May, and June. Did you see or encounter Commander Pandurevic in the area of Zvornik or Mali Zvornik during those three months?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Bourgon. I noticed Mr. Sarapa wishing to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question has been translated wrongly into B/C/S. Mr. Bourgon's question was this: "When it comes to Commander Pandurevic, I suggest to you that when he did arrive in the Zvornik area, he came to be in command of a regular unit." And the translation that we heard implied that the witness arrived there, and that is why the witness's answer was somewhat illogical. Could the witness be read the question again, the question that is on line 12, between lines 6 and 9?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon. You've heard what Mr. Sarapa said. If you could attend to that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Indeed, I missed that because I'm looking at the transcript at the same time, and the question that appeared was the one that I posed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to ask this question once again, and the question is that: When Mr. Pandurevic arrived in the Zvornik area, I suggest to you that it was to be in command of a regular military unit of the VRS; namely, the Zvornik Brigade. Can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, finally, I have a last question with Commander Pandurevic before moving on. I suggested to you yesterday that Commander Pandurevic was pretty well in control of the Zvornik Brigade in 1995, and your response was: "I think so." Now, I refer my colleagues to page 915, lines 21 to 25. I then suggested to you that Commander Pandurevic was exercising effective control over that brigade. Of course, what I meant then, as I explained a few lines later, is that Commander Pandurevic put the military situation in Zvornik in order when he arrived. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that Mr. Pandurevic was respected as an officer in the area of Zvornik. I can say that based on comments by the civilians and the troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. I move on to seeking clarification concerning a question about Drago Nikolic. I asked you yesterday whether you could share with us some names of the people from the brigade who had mentioned information to you concerning Drago Nikolic, and your answer was: It was too long ago and you cannot remember. I'd just like to know if you can tell us today some members of the Zvornik Brigade that you remember from the period 1992-1995, other than Commander Pandurevic and Deputy Commander Obrenovic. Any other names that you remember having any dealings with from the Zvornik Brigade Command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, I asked you some questions in relation to your background.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think we need to go into private session for this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to confirm something that you discussed with the Prosecution during your examination-in-chief; and, basically, the Prosecution asked you if, by the time of your second trip -- now, remember yesterday that's why I discussed with you the three events, so the second trip is the one that would have allegedly taken place 30 days after the first one. And the question from the Prosecution was: "Had you heard any information concerning the fate of the Muslim men from Srebrenica?" And your answer was the following, and I quote from page 770, lines 22 to 23: "Well, we didn't have any information about what was happening then." Do you stick with this testimony today, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The next question that was asked by my colleague was the following: "Did you ever receive any information that there had been mass executions of men in the Zvornik area?" Your answer, on page 771, lines 1 and 2, was the following: "We learnt of that later on in the ensuing period when the public got to know about it." Do you stick with this testimony today, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You were then asked, in your view, when the public began to learn about these mass executions, and you answered at page 771, line 5: "Well, I can't remember exactly how much time went by." Do you stick with this testimony today, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, on the basis of these three questions that were posed to you by the Prosecution, I'd like to ask you a question of mine, which is the following: Is it your testimony today that when you returned for a second time, allegedly, at the Zvornik Brigade Command with your friend, you did not have information that Muslim men from Srebrenica had been executed in the Zvornik area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't, no, and I cannot say anything about my friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, just to try and find out -- to follow up on this answer of yours, I'd like to know if you had any information in July of 1995 that there was a column of men from Srebrenica trying to join Tuzla by the woods and that they posed a threat to Zvornik and the complete Zvornik area. Were you aware of this, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard it on the news, but I didn't know whether Zvornik came under any threat or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And my last question on this topic is: Was there, to your knowledge or your recollection, any type of security alert in relation to what was going on in the Zvornik area in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could tell from the comments that something was happening, but I was not fully aware of the situation. I didn't know exactly what that was all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Let's go back for a few minutes to the situation in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we can move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Bourgon. Let's move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like now to go quickly over the events of your first alleged visit to Zvornik Brigade Command, and first to try and determine how much time this event lasted for. So let's go together over the steps,

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: (redacted) Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer. One moment, sir, before you answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're in open session;, and to be on the safe side we may want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he's correct. He is correct. I think we need to --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I have no difficulty in going in private session. I'm just trying to do my best to do what we can in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's do it this way: Let's redact the second part, second half of line 4 to line 6, before the last sentence. And I suggest that we go, just for this answer, in private session, or we can stay in open session, he can say it, and we'll redact it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I have about four questions that we can go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In private session. It's safer to go in private session. Let's go in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Can you ask if we can go to 10.45, instead of stopping at 10.30 or 10.40, whenever they tell us? Okay. Thank you. Go ahead, please. We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, I go back to my question. When you arrive at Zvornik Brigade Command allegedly on that morning with your friend, what's the first thing that you saw when you -- with the car, before entering any building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a guard shed or lodge at the entrance, where the gate was, and that was a soldier. And my friend got out and said he wanted to see Mr. Pandurevic, and he pointed us in the direction of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So there was a soldier at the gate. Is that the soldier that you referred to earlier in your testimony or a different soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other soldier at the entrance to the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So we're talking about two soldiers: One at the gate and one more in the building. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I take it that you did not drive -- did the soldier have to open a gate to let you in? Do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whether it was open or shut; but when we arrived at the gate, the soldier came up to us, and my friend said that he wanted to go to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what does -- what did this soldier would have said to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He pointed us in the direction of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you don't recall, I take it, any ramp that you would have to go over to get to that building. Do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know there was a gate. Now, whether the gate was open or closed, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to describe the building as you go in, the building itself, the hallway. What do you recall from the hallway of the building when you went in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the entrance to the building is from the parking lot. The entrance is in the middle; and when you enter the building, you go up the stairs, from the hallway up the stairs to the first floor, and that's where we came across a soldier who escorted us to Mr. Pandurevic's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So I take it, sir, that the soldier that you went -- that you met inside, he was on the first floor. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And given the fact that -- so I take it, then, that in the hallway itself, before going up the stairs to the first floor, you did not see anybody there. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the top of the staircase on the first floor, we saw a soldier. We headed towards him, we approached him, and we told him where we were going.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But my question, sir, is: In the hallway, before going up the stairs, you did not see any soldiers there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you did not see any reception point there, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you don't recall being asked to sign any book for visitors, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were not asked to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I go back. Can you describe the hallway before going up the stairs? What does the hallway look like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entrance door, a wide corridor, and a staircase leading up to the first floor. Maybe ten metres long and five metres wide was that corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, given that this was the first time that you physically went to the Zvornik Brigade Command, I suggest to you that there was no way you could know, or why would you go to the first floor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that that question contains characterisations which are contrary to the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, if my colleague can refer me to what testimony it is contrary to.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'd be glad to do that, Mr. President. I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you can rephrase the question and ask the witness, "How did you know where you needed to go?" I think otherwise it becomes a storm in a teacup, unnecessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, no one told you to go up to the first floor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My friend most probably knew where Mr. Pandurevic's office was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But the guard duty at the gate did not tell you where the commander's office was, he only indicated to you where the Command building was; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, again, to come back on the hallway, I suggest to you, sir, that, in that hallway, there are offices around and that there were people in those offices. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible, but we did not see anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So it is your testimony today that the entire ground floor was empty, that you basically could walk into the Zvornik Brigade Command without anyone saying anything to you, and then going to the first floor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no soldiers on the ground floor or on the first floor; but at the entrance, there was a soldier who told us where to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But you testified, sir, that that soldier, you met him on the first floor. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So how many soldiers are we talking about? Now, if I look at your testimony, it would now appear that there's one at the gate, one at the entrance, and one on the first floor. Is it one, two, or three soldiers that you met on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two soldiers: One at the entrance at the gate, and one on the first floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So I am correct in saying that, in the entrance to the Command, according to your testimony, that is, the hallway before going up the stairs, there was absolutely nobody there. You could walk into the Zvornik Brigade Command, and go up to the first floor without anyone asking you for any identity card or any other information as to what you were doing there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, sir, I suggest to you that this is not possible, based on the information we have, but that we will present that later in the case. But let's go back to the first floor. You meet this soldier, and you mentioned that he was on duty. What kind of duty soldier was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was just on duty in that hallway.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Please explain what you mean by "duty," and how you can testify that he was on duty. What was he doing that you know he was on duty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was present in the hallway. I don't know what his tasks were.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And describe that soldier for us, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a long time ago, and all the soldiers wore the same uniform. I can't remember. I know that he wore a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did he have any distinctive sign? Was he tall? Was he short? Was he fat? Was he skinny? Did he have grey hair? Anything you remember for us, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was neither tall, nor short, neither fat, nor skinny. He was average, of an average weight, and I really can't remember. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And he was the only person that you could see on the complete first floor; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And it is at that moment that Drago Nikolic would have appeared, coming out of an office or just coming back or coming by, as you testified; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, was he coming out of an office or did he just pop by?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly whether he was coming out of somewhere or he just came by. In any case, as we were returning from Mr. Pandurevic's office, we saw him at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you saw him after going to Mr. Pandurevic's office, so then you know where that office is. Where is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As you go upstairs, you go to the right, and then it is on the left-hand side on the first floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He explained this yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, but there will be more questions with respect to the location of the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, when you went to Mr. Pandurevic's office, is it at the end of the hall or is it just close to the stairway?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a bit further from the staircase, on the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So it is neither at the end of either side of that hallway; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember whether it was the last office or one before last. I can't remember exactly at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And where is that soldier at that time? You went straight to the office of Mr. Pandurevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We followed the soldier. The soldier opened Mr. Pandurevic's office. He saw that there was nobody in, then he looked to the other side, where Obrenovic was. There was nobody there, either, and then we followed him back. At that moment, Mr. Nikolic either came by or had come out of his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, that soldier, he never told you Mr. Pandurevic is not there. He had to look in those two offices to see if he was there; is that correct? That's your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He had to check. He opened the door of the office. He saw that there was nobody there, and he told us that there was nobody there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think the time is correct to take a short break, and then we can continue after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. First of all, I would like to thank the staff for agreeing to go beyond 10.30 until now. There will be a 25-minute break starting from now. Unfortunately, something urgent has cropped up, a personal urgent matter that I have to attend to, so I will have to leave. I don't know if I will make it on time to come back. I don't know. That's the position, but probably not. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, may we have a time estimate from our friends? We have a witness who is on standby.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will take the full next session, an hour and a half, and I'll be done, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You still wish to cross-examine this witness, Mr. Ostojic, given the extensive cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I've shortened it a little bit, Mr. President, but I think we'll be able to finish him today. I'm not going to ask that he come back. I'll try my best to make sure he gets done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you could, the remaining ones, coordinate a little bit with Mr. Bourgon and see if one could shorten a little bit and try and finish with this witness today, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, may we release the pending witness, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think, from the looks of it, we don't need him now here, but please keep him here over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Oh, absolutely, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As was indicated by Judge Agius, we'll be sitting pursuant to 15 bis. I hope the parties have sorted out a way to finish the examination of this witness today.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We'll do our best, Mr. President. I'm sure we can succeed in doing so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Welcome back, Witness. I have a few more questions with respect to what happened on that first floor, allegedly, as you stated in your testimony. First, I'd like to know how you, yourself, were dressed on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And maybe, Mr. President, we ought to go into private session again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, in any event, based on the timings that you shared with us today, I would imagine that your friend leaving immediately after, that means that he left before noon. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it was before noon, but it wasn't in the afternoon, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, your friend did not tell you why he left immediately for Belgrade, did he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And your friend did not inform you whether he had a meeting to attend to or any other urgent obligation in Belgrade, did he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't say anything, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, during the time that you allegedly were at the Zvornik Brigade Command, your friend did not ask for the location of Commander Pandurevic or Obrenovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't. It was just the soldier that said that there was nobody there, and he didn't comment where he was. We didn't get an answer as to where he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, I take it that you cannot confirm and you don't know whether your friend asked for a phone number to try and reach the commander by phone.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He didn't ask for the phone number.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, you know that either the commander or the deputy commander of a brigade, based on your background, can always be reached by the duty officer or by his Command, and you know that no steps were taken in this regard; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, because Mr. Nikolic turned up, and then there was no need to look for Mr. Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, sir, your friend did not attempt to contact anyone that day in your presence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, your friend did not attempt to contact higher up in the chain of command of the military, for example, the corps, did he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, except for Mr. Nikolic, nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, your friend did not attempt to find Commander Pandurevic physically while he was with you, did he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, we've established that your friend knew Obrenovic very well, in fact, much better than Pandurevic, but you can't help us with whether your friend looked for Obrenovic that day, physically, did he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it was established that Mr. Pandurevic wasn't there, we looked for Obrenovic. And when we found out that Obrenovic wasn't there, then Mr. Nikolic turned up, and that was the contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, would you agree with me that this is the first time that you mention that you looked for Obrenovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's just not consistent with the prior testimony of this witness. He's misstating the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We heard what he said. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, in your presence, no one -- your friend did not ask whether and if it was possible to contact Obrenovic by phone or by radio, did he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, you -- it is quite obvious that our case today is that there was never any such conversation or visit to the Zvornik Brigade, as you allege there was, but I'll suggest to you why this is so and ask you to comment. First of all, I would suggest to you, sir, that your friend knew both Commander Pandurevic and Mr. Obrenovic, that your presence was not required to meet them on that day. Would you agree with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did know, but we didn't know whether we were supposed to meet them or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, I suggest to you that, for example, if your friend wanted to have, let's say, a witness of some kind, he would have, as a minimum, told you what it is that he believed was happening and that he wanted to prevent, and he did not. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, if your -- again, if your friend wanted to have some kind of a witness to his visit to try and prevent bad things, I suggest to you, sir, that he would not have met with Drago Nikolic alone while you were waiting outside. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what he wanted, but it was a private conversation, going privately, not pursuant to anybody's order. My friend simply wanted to go there and to meet Mr. Pandurevic; and since he wasn't there, he met Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, if your friend needed somebody to accompany him to Zvornik Brigade Command, again, as you say, to try and prevent some bad things, would you agree with me that he would have provided you with the full details of that conversation, so that you could take notes and there could be a record made of the event? Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that my friend, even if he wanted to do that -- well, whether he informed someone or not, I don't know. But if he felt the need to do so, then he informed his superior officers or somebody else. I don't know whether he wrote about this or whether he, in fact, did inform them. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, I suggest to you that if your friend wanted to have somebody or needed somebody to accompany him, he would not have taken someone who had no authority whatsoever to intervene in Zvornik, someone who was forbidden to even cross over to Zvornik, and someone he would have to justify the presence in Zvornik. Would you agree with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what the intention was. I think my friend wanted to learn what was happening in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, if your friend really wanted to go to the Zvornik Brigade Command to prevent bad things, as you say, I suggest to you that he would not have left immediately for Belgrade the same day, without taking any concrete action. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what he intended.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And I say that if your friend needed somebody to accompany him, and if his intention was to try and prevent any things, as you say, he would have insisted on getting the contact details of either the commander or the deputy commander, whom he knew very well, to try and meet them, which pursuant to your testimony he did not do. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't try to do that. Well, he did, by his very arrival. But since he didn't find them there, then he didn't do anything to try and find him --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: to try and find them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, in fact, on the basis of all of the above, I suggest to you that the fact that he did not share the information he wanted to tell Pandurevic before the visit, the fact that he did not share with you any specific information or the details of the meeting he allegedly had with Drago Nikolic after, and for all the details we covered together this morning, it makes it clear that this visit never took place. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't comment his meeting, but my friend did visit, he did meet with Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, we move on to the alleged second visit to the Zvornik Brigade Command. At what time of the day did this visit take place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the day, but I can't remember whether it was in the morning or in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, who did you meet in the Zvornik Brigade Command that second visit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the entrance, my friend asked for Mr. Pandurevic or Obrenovic. Since neither were there, we turned back.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, what did they tell you about the location of Commander Pandurevic or Deputy Commander Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They simply told us that they were not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, that soldier you spoke on that day, was he on the ground floor or on the first floor, like your first visit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you stopped at the gate, and the soldier at the gate knew that both the commander and the deputy commander were not there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, sir, I tell you that this is not possible, but that's not the main question. The main question is: How come the first soldier you met for the first alleged visit did not know that the commander or the deputy commander was not there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that he didn't know, since he never informed us at the gate that the two were not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So if he did not inform you that they were there, he just let you in? Is that what he did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, I further suggest to you that on the basis of what you recall from that second visit, it's further evidence that the first alleged visit never took place. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, once again, you don't know what it is, based on your testimony, that that second visit would have been about, what exactly your friend was looking for; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but he always said that since he hailed from the area of Zvornik, that he wanted to be informed about what was going on in his municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And by meaning his municipality and what is going on, it has nothing to do with bad things; would that be correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, my friend has referred specifically to this witness's testimony with respect to this topic, and he is misstating what this witness has said previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could rephrase your question, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Will do, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Witness, at page 768, lines 14 to 16, the question was: "And was this the only trip you and your friend took to this place?" Answer, lines 15 and 16: "Well, later on we went one more time, looking for Vinko and Obrenovic, but we did not find either of them, so we returned." "Do you recall what the purpose of this second trip was?" "The same purpose, that my friend should gain more information about what was happening in the Zvornik area, but he didn't comment about what." Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not provide any comment as to why he wanted to get in touch, and that was also another private visit and another attempt to try and get together with either Mr. Pandurevic or Mr. Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And later on lines 12 and 13, you say: "I think he wanted to prevent all the bad things, and he condemned any crime if it occurred." But you don't know whether this statement applies, yes or no, to that second visit, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are no comments about the second visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, I go back to the events of 1992, and, again, I'd like to give you an opportunity to come back and say that you were involved in these events. And I'll ask you to confirm the information we received from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I refer my friend to a statement dated the 14th of March, 2001, on page 2, and I take it that this is sufficient for him to know the name of the person I'm talking about, the second one on the list that I provided him with.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, this witness said the following: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe we need to go in private session and redact the last part. I thought we were in private session. I apologise, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, I conclude my cross-examination simply by saying that, on the basis of your testimony, I don't doubt that you were in a relationship with your friend, but I put it to you that this alleged visit in 1995, the first alleged visit, never took place and that it is a fabrication to help your friend. Would you agree with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that my friend and I went to see Mr. Nikolic. It is no fabrication at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Mr. President, I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Who is next? Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, this may go in the category of "no good deed goes unpunished," but I want to make sure of one thing before we move on to the other cross-examinations and my redirect, which will be brief. We have advised my friend, and I don't think it's any secret, that we intend to -- and perhaps the witness should remove his ear phones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Witness, could you do that, could you take off your headphones, please? He said he did not understand English.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We have advised our friends that we do intend to offer the prior statement of testimony of the friend, pursuant to 92 quater. We've advised my friend of this. We've advised, I think, everyone else of this. I just want to make sure that with that knowledge, my friend has conducted the cross-examination he considers sufficient and appropriate, so that we would not be in the position where we might have to bring this witness back once the motion is filed. I presume that the cross-examination was conducted with that in mind, but I wanted to make sure so that we don't run into this problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any say to this, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes. I do wish to respond, Mr. President. First of all, my friend did not advise us of his intention to call the testimony of the friend, pursuant to Rule 92 quater. In fact, the Prosecution filed a detailed motion, saying that it had reviewed all the evidence in the case and requested the permission of the Trial Chamber to make a number of changes in its case, including the addition of new witnesses, the withdrawal of a number of witnesses, and the possible request to ask the Trial Chamber for the testimony of three witnesses to be included pursuant to Rule 92 quater. Witness 102, as he is known unofficially, who is the friend, there was never any request put forward by the Prosecution to say that it is testimony that they would request to put it in on the record. Now, we approach the Prosecution, no longer at the end of examination-in-chief of this witness, and say, in the end we have to go and get it because it's not coming towards us, "What is your intention with respect to the person known as 102?" And it is then that we are informed, after the examination-in-chief, that the Prosecution intends to get this testimony in. I believe, and my friends here on this side can confirm, that they have never been aware of this fact, that it is completely new. That being said, Mr. President, when that motion is filed, and if we believe there is a need to recall this witness, then we will for sure ask the Trial Chamber for leave to recall this witness. But we don't think that will be necessary, and we think there will be no basis whatsoever to admit the evidence of Witness 102. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just wanted to confirm what my colleague just said. We were never informed that the testimony of the witness or the statement of the Witness 102, 92 quater, introduced into the file pursuant to Rule 92.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber wishes to leave the matter as it is now, and we'll deal with it when and if it arises. But if you have any further to say, we'll entertain it. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour, I agree with what my learned friend Ms. Fauveau has just said. But rather more to the point, until such time as, one, the motion is submitted and, two, has been ruled upon, it's not really fair to say that Defence counsel should conduct a cross-examination based on something that hasn't yet happened; and in particular, in particular, in fact, there's been no ruling on the point. It's not so much the fact there may be a motion; it's the ruling that's going to be important, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Point taken. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, it is your turn now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I believe so, Your Honour. With your leave, I'll proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, my name is John Ostojic. I represent Ljubisa Beara in these proceedings here. I'm going to ask you a series of questions, sir, this afternoon. First of all, I would like to know, yesterday you discussed with us something you coined as a civic duty; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And for counsel, it's on page 62, line 19.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you correct me if I'm wrong, i think you mentioned that after, when you got this second call to meet with the Prosecutor in 2006, you had no idea why he was calling, what he was calling about. You just felt you needed to go because it was your civic duty; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, I take it, sir, that you had this commitment to civic duty prior to 2006 as well, like in 2002, for example. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And, sir, explain this to me: If you had this commitment of civic duty, when you talked to the Prosecutor on November 27, 2002, explain to me why you failed to inform them or mention to them about this purported encounter and visit you claim occurred in the Zvornik Brigade Command.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, the visit did not take place. It was not at that time the visit took place in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'll try again, because I think we may have misunderstood each other, sir, just so I can get these parameters set and so that we're on the same page with everyone. Your first visit ever with a Prosecutor of the ICTY was on or about the 27th of November, 2002; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And your second interview, as I think we've established already, was the 21st of July, 2006; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you, sir, after 1995, about the time that you had this first meeting with the Prosecutor in 2002, as well as during your meeting with the Prosecutor, as well as the three or so years after that meeting with the Prosecutor, what happened to your commitment to civic duty? Why didn't you inform the Prosecutor about this purported encounter or information that you had regarding this visit at the Zvornik Brigade Command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't asked about that event at the time, and I just did not remember to mention it spontaneously. The second time, when the gentleman from the Office of the Prosecutor reminded me of that event, then I spoke about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, did you know, sir, in the year 2002, whether or not there were any investigations regarding the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you know, sir, on or about that late 2002, November 27th, approximately, 2002, that there were trials that were undergoing in connection with the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything I know comes from the media, and I don't -- I can't remember when that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And you followed the media rather closely, I take it, is that correct, at that time, 2000, November?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever work with a person by the name of Zoran Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know who he is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My friend knew him. I believe that Zoran was Dragan's brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever meet with Zoran at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, if your friend, who you saw from time to time or monthly, do you know if he ever visited with Zoran Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he visited him, but I know that my friend and Dragan spoke about the latter's brother, and then my friend learned that he, indeed, had a brother affiliated with the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, what role, if any, did you play in Dragan Obrenovic's defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't play any role.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about your friend, did he play any role in Dragan Obrenovic's defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. He didn't comment about that. If he did go to testify, then possibly he did comment about his friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, help us with this information: Who is the chief of the Zvornik police in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember exactly now who the chief was. They rotated. Several of them changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, sir, who was the commander of the Zvornik police in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. A couple of them changed places, so I don't know who was occupying that post at what time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just for the next question, Mr. President, if I may just go into private session for a couple questions or moments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just out of caution. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, did they, meaning the Prosecutors, ask you to look in any documents you may have in order to corroborate or verify this claim about this encounter that you had in July of 1995, purportedly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They didn't ask me for any document, and I didn't have any documents, in fact, and they didn't ask for any, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, in this place where you worked at that time -- and we're trying to be as general as possible so that we can stay in open session and not reveal anything that we're not allowed to. The place where you worked, sir, how many people were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 15 to 20, at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you have an assistant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but all of them had retired and --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You're not suggesting that the day you went purportedly to Zvornik Brigade Command, everybody retired that day, are you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not saying that, but at that time I might have been on my own, because before that the commander and deputy and assistant had retired; and of the senior officers, I was left alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, sorry to interrupt, but whenever you find it is a convenient time, we would break.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I can just have two more minutes or one minute, I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you have a secretary at that time, July of 1995, or did she also retire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. It's a small office; no secretary at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just one other question, sir. In July of 1995, to the best of your recollection, how many people worked in the same offices where you worked? Can you give us a best-case estimate on that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I mean, I think it was asked and answered, "About 15 to 20."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I thought he did, but then he mentioned his assistant, who subsequently seemed to have retired or thereabouts. So it might be repetitive, but I think I needed clarity based on some of the answers that he has offered. So all I am looking for is for him to clarify it, not to have him say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, if we can move on. If you could rephrase your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Witness, I'm a little bit confused as to how many people worked in the same office as you did in July of 1995, and I know you told us ten to 15. Do you stand by that testimony, that ten to 15 people worked in your offices in July of 1995, given that seemingly most of them retired?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Fifteen to 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fifteen to 20, I misspoke when I heard my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fifteen to 20. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And can you give us the names of your deputies?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Or maybe this should be in private session? Why don't we do this? We'll take a break right now, with the Court's permission, and proceed after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Given that it is Friday today and there is a session ahead, so I would suggest to take only a 15-minute break now, with the indulgence of the interpreters and the court reporters. I checked that with the audio/video unit, so we'll break for 15 minutes, and I would very much ask the parties to sort out how they will finish with the examination of this witness during the break. Fifteen minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I want to go back to a question I asked you regarding the Prosecutor informing you that there was no documentary evidence whatsoever, which recorded any visit you and your friend may have had purportedly in July of 1995, and your answer is on on line 34, it looks like page 75, where you state: "Before this trial, in a previous meeting, they did tell me." And my question, just to follow up on that, sir: Can you share with us who gave you this information and what specifically they told you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember who it was; but when talking to me in my place of residence, they asked me about the event, about when I went to the Command with my friend, and I told them about it. I told what -- them what I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm more interested, sir, in finding out whether you tried to look for any documentary evidence to help the Prosecutor in proving what I think is an occurrence that did not happen. Did you go back, sir, to your place of employment at any time and search through your documents to see if there's any notation from a secretary, an assistant, a deputy, or any other personnel that would verify where your whereabouts were on any given day in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember very well that I went there with my friend. That's a fact. I have no reason to say anything different, but I didn't keep any records or any notation, nor did I have a secretary for her to make any notations.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, when you leave your place of employment in 1995, given the title that you had, wouldn't it have been customary for you to advise someone that you were going in a different country, for example, or a different republic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think we're in open session, in which case we would need a redaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I agree. Shall we continue, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I wasn't going to has him the name; I just wanted to know if he told anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you know if your friend who was purportedly with you in July of 1995, who made this alleged visit to the Zvornik Brigade Command, do you know if he informed any of his superiors as to whether or not he was going to another republic or country?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know if the Prosecutor ever shared with you that they obtained his notes, or his diary, or records that he or his brother may have had? Do you know if they obtained that documentation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Explain this to me, sir: Given your experience, and we're talking about your experience and your education that you just shared with us briefly, does it seem somewhat odd to you, if you will, that the place where you claim you went to, there's no evidence whatsoever of you showing up there. And the place where you departed from during your place of employment, there was, likewise, no evidence to suggest that you had a meeting or advised anyone in writing that you were going across a border to another country. And then if you add to that this third person, your friend, that likewise there's no evidence that he informed anyone that he was going to another country to find out if there were bad things going on. Do you find that, given your history and your experience, particularly odd, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had we gone officially to these talks, then there would be a trace and there would be a written note, but it was a private trip, and that was not recorded. As for my friend, I don't know whether he made any notes or not and whether he informed anyone or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, I'm not suggesting that it was a formal trip that you took; but given that it was a private trip, would you have advised anyone privately that you would be going to another country to make this private trip? I mean, sir, you'll agree with me, typically, we would inform our, let's say, spouses, our close family friends, if we're going to another country or even across the border where there happens to be a war and that, "I might be exposed to some danger." And you're telling this Court that you did not inform anyone of that, other than you told your deputy you'll be gone for a little while? Is that what you want us to believe?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't tell anyone because I thought that I was going privately with my friend, and he worked in MUP. If necessary, he would inform his senior officers thereof.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, we're going to talk about some of your assumptions in a minute, sir, but let me ask you this: In the area that you and your friend were coming from, was there a war going on right there in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And how about in July of 1995, do you remember the place that you and your friend were going to? Do you know if there was a war going on there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the town of Zvornik, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And, sir, do you know if your friend, who came with you to this purported trip, do you know if he was armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether he was armed or not, what he had. He was wearing civilian clothes, and I didn't notice any arms on him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, now I want to go back to this written material that we talked about that doesn't exist from either you, personally, the place of employment where you worked; your friend, personally, his place of employment; and also the place where you purportedly went on this July 1995. Am I correct, sir, that you knew there was no written material, because that's was told us the Prosecutor told you; and having known that, you therefore knew that you could say anything because no one could verify what you claim to be the truth; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-108 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Prosecutor did not tell us whether he did or didn't have a document. He just asked about the event, and I answered him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
